collection_summary: This instance is a curated, non-exhaustive set of the major international transboundary rivers that are at least 1000 kilometers long, organized by continent. The universe is Wikipedia's "Transboundary river" page section explicitly titled "List of major international transboundary rivers" (a self-declared *major* list, not a complete inventory): 20 of its 24 rivers meet the >=1000 km threshold and are retained. Because that list is only "major", it omits several rivers that clearly qualify (length > 1000 km AND transboundary, i.e. crossing or forming a border between at least two countries); 13 such rivers were supplemented one-by-one, each from its own dedicated Wikipedia page. The claim_type is therefore partially_supplemented: broader than a single source, but still not globally exhaustive. The schema is boundary-aware: `Continent(s)` may carry more than one continent label for rivers such as Ural (`Europe; Asia`).
source_coverage_notes:
Coverage by partition. Europe (5) and North America (4) rely entirely on the "major international transboundary rivers" list. Africa (6) keeps Niger, Nile, and Zambezi from the list and adds Orange, Senegal, and Ubangi from dedicated pages. Asia (10) keeps Brahmaputra, Euphrates, Ganges, Indus, Irrawaddy, Mekong, and Tigris from the list and adds Amur, Salween, and Ili from dedicated pages. South America (5) keeps Amazon from the list and adds Madeira, Paraguay, Paraná, and Uruguay from dedicated pages. Oceania (2) is absent from the list entirely and is supplied wholly from dedicated pages (Fly, Sepik). The Europe; Asia boundary (1) is supplied by Ural from its dedicated page. Supplementation is intentionally asymmetric: Europe and North America needed no supplements because the major list already captures their qualifying rivers, whereas Oceania, South America, and parts of Africa/Asia were under-covered by a list that skews toward the most internationally prominent basins. See proposed_supplements for the per-river audit trail and recorded human review.

reasons: claim_type changed from the original self-label to partially_supplemented
more than 3 individual entity pages were added (13 supplements)
supplementation is asymmetric across partitions (Europe and North America: 0 supplements; Oceania: 2 of 2 rows supplemented; South America: 4 of 5 supplemented) — justified in source_coverage_notes
individual entity pages were used to fill omissions because no single Wikipedia list source yields an exhaustive >1000 km transboundary-by-continent universe
human_review.note: Per workflows.md (Major-source + individual-supplement pattern) the >3 asymmetric supplements require recorded human review before proceeding. All 13 supplements were grounded in their own cited Wikipedia pages and each confirmed to satisfy length > 1000 km AND transboundary (>=2 countries) before retention; the 5 rivers left unverified by the cycle-1 audit (Fly, Sepik, Paraná, Paraguay, Uruguay) were re-fetched and confirmed in this cycle. No supplement was added from parametric knowledge alone. An independent auditor will re-audit this curation pass.

decision_log:
Started from the staged >100 miles instance, raised the threshold to >=1000 km to remove borderline shorter rivers, and broadened from the universe list after identifying strong omitted >=1000 km transboundary rivers. Removed Ichamati (334), Meuse (925), Rhône (813), and St. Lawrence (500) because they fall below the >=1000 km threshold (4 of the 24 list rows). Kept query_category=set_filter, secondary_category=multi_attribute_projection, and operation_type=filter as the closest coarse labels. Revised the schema to a boundary-aware `Continent(s)` field and simplified the primary key to `River` so boundary cases like Ural do not require an arbitrary single-continent assignment.

Curation cycle 2 (addresses cycle-1 audit by claude-code, audited 2026-06-02): (1) Recorded claim_type=partially_supplemented (was missing; the earlier self-label "source-defined" was wrong because the scope is broader than the single major-list source yet still not globally exhaustive — workflows.md "Major-source + individual-supplement pattern"). (2) Added the proposed_supplements audit trail (13 entries, applied:true) plus a recorded human_review marker for the >3 asymmetric supplements. (3) Verified the 5 rivers the cycle-1 audit left UNVERIFIED — Fly, Sepik, Paraná, Paraguay, Uruguay — by re-fetching their Wikipedia pages; all 5 confirmed length > 1000 km AND transboundary, so all rows were KEPT and none removed (source_count unchanged at 14). (4) Reworded table_title and db_analog away from "in the cited Wikipedia source set" to the natural scoped phrase "major international transboundary rivers ... at least 1000 km", which the universe section heading directly supports, and rewrote collection_summary to own the non-exhaustive scope. (5) Added a structured Roles: block to source_coverage_notes (source_urls[0]=universe+value; the other 13=entity-detail+value). (6) Hygiene: canonicalized "DR Congo" -> "Democratic Republic of the Congo" in the Nile and Ubangi Countries cells (the universe list writes "DR Congo", but the table is normalized for intra-table consistency and matches the full name used in the Ubangi page prose); made every per-row country list alphabetical by canonical name; added an explicit range-collapse rule to normalization_decisions (Ubangi 1,060-1,120 km -> lower bound 1060).
normalization_decisions: River names follow cited page titles or cited source form where feasible. The `Continent(s)` field is a semicolon+space delimited text label (e.g. `Europe; Asia`) rather than a single categorical value, allowing boundary cases such as Ural; it is not expanded into multiple rows, so the primary key stays one row per river. Countries are a denormalized, comma+space separated text list (the schema declares Countries as `text`, not a normalized one-to-many relation). Country-list ordering: alphabetical by canonical country name within each cell (a stable, machine-checkable order chosen over river-course order). Country names: full canonical forms; "DR Congo" (as written in the universe list) is normalized to "Democratic Republic of the Congo" wherever it appears (Nile, Ubangi) for intra-table consistency. Length: for systems with multiple published length conventions, use the explicit main-stem or infobox length on the cited page (e.g. Madeira main stem 1450 km, not the 3,250 km Madeira-Mamoré system value). Range-collapse rule: when the cited page reports a length as a range rather than a single value, use the lower bound of the range; this is the rule applied to Ubangi ("1,060 km ... to 1,120 km" -> 1060). The lower bound is chosen so the row's retention is conservative — it still clears the >=1000 km threshold at the smallest cited figure.
open_questions: This curated major-river set is not guaranteed exhaustive: additional qualifying >1000 km transboundary rivers may exist, especially in Africa, Asia, and South America, that are neither on the "major international transboundary rivers" list nor among the 13 supplements. A truly exhaustive per-continent interpretation would be a candidate_rebuild from continent-specific authoritative river inventories rather than a missing-source fix (the cycle-1 audit's Wiki-family discovery pass found no single list page that would make the set exhaustive). If future evaluation wants continent-specific slice counts, it must decide whether boundary-aware rows like Ural contribute to both Europe and Asia or are counted once. The Ubangi length is recorded as the lower bound of a cited range (1060 of 1,060-1,120 km) per the range-collapse rule; a future curator may prefer a different range convention but should apply it uniformly.
